answers.gloss: A traffic-engineering node in a layer-specific TE topology; it is specifically a TE abstraction of resources/functions at that layer, rather than an unconstrained generic forwarding-domain node.
answers.example: ROADM R1 represented as a node in the optical or OTN layer network.
answers.relations: It is part of i.tetopo; i.tp, i.ttp, i.tcep, and i.cmatrix may be located on it, while i.telink connects such nodes.

answers.gloss: A node-owned termination point at which a TE link terminates.
answers.example: The R1 termination point facing R2 on the R1-R2 TE link.
answers.relations: It is on i.tenode and terminates i.telink. Unlike i.ttp, it terminates a topological TE link rather than serving as the head or endpoint of an end-to-end TE tunnel.

answers.gloss: The adaptation/supporting relationship by which a client-layer TP is supported by a server-layer TP; despite its label, the modeled concept is the support relationship rather than merely another ordinary TP.
answers.example: An OTN TP at R1 supported by an optical-layer TP at R1.
answers.relations: It relates termination points across client/server layers and supports i.tp; it represents layer adaptation rather than an adjacency between nodes.

answers.gloss: The point at which a TE tunnel originates or terminates—a tunnel trail head.
answers.example: The A1 trail head of the A1-A3 ODU2 tunnel.
answers.relations: It is on i.tenode and originates or terminates i.tunnel. It is a tunnel endpoint, not inherently an external customer/service access point, although an implementation could associate one with such access.

answers.gloss: An end-to-end traffic-engineered tunnel that realizes connectivity for a service.
answers.example: The A1-A3 ODU2 TE tunnel.
answers.relations: It runs between i.ttp endpoints, traverses i.tetopo, may contain endpoint representations such as i.tcep, and may be labeled by i.otnlabel. It is primarily an internal TE construct, though it realizes a service.

answers.gloss: An OTN TE label expressing the tributary-slot/TPN multiplexing assignment and structure used to carry a client ODU in a server OTN signal.
answers.example: The TS/TPN allocation carrying an ODU2 within an OTU4.
answers.relations: It labels i.tunnel. It describes a concrete allocatable multiplexing assignment/resource, not merely a generic declaration that the layer protocol is OTN or ODU2.

answers.gloss: A node's matrix of permitted internal connectivity, expressing which relevant termination points or switching sides may be connected.
answers.example: R2's matrix allowing specified ingress TPs to be cross-connected to specified egress TPs.
answers.relations: It is located on i.tenode and constrains internal switching/cross-connection possibilities; it is not an inter-node link.

answers.gloss: A traffic-engineering topological adjacency between TE nodes within a layer network.
answers.example: The R1-R2 TE link.
answers.relations: It lies in i.tetopo, connects i.tenode instances, and is terminated at node-owned i.tp instances.

answers.gloss: A per-layer traffic-engineering network/topology.
answers.example: The OTN layer network containing R1, R2, R3, and their OTN TE links.
answers.relations: It contains i.tenode and i.telink and is traversed by i.tunnel. Each instance is necessarily layer-specific in this model; a multi-layer domain would be represented through multiple related per-layer topologies, not one undifferentiated instance.

answers.gloss: An endpoint of a tunnel connection represented within or on a node.
answers.example: The A1-A3 tunnel's connection endpoint on R1.
answers.relations: It is on i.tenode and part of i.tunnel. It differs from i.tp, which terminates a TE link, and from i.ttp, which denotes the overall tunnel trail head.

answers.gloss: A forwarding node or forwarding domain in the single multi-layer topology. It is not restricted to a layer-specific TE abstraction.
answers.example: ROADM R1, represented once in the OTN-over-optical domain.
answers.relations: It is part of t.topo; t.ltp, t.sip, t.cep, t.nrg, and t.translink may be associated with or located on it, and t.link runs between such nodes.

answers.gloss: A node-owned edge point at which a topological link terminates; it is distinct from service-access and connection endpoints.
answers.example: The R1 edge point facing R2 on the R1-R2 link.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and terminates t.link.

answers.gloss: An explicit link-like representation of client/server layer adaptation at a node.
answers.example: The OTU4-to-ODU2 adaptation at R1.
answers.relations: It is located at t.node and expresses adaptation involving the multiplexing/layer structure described by t.lpq. It is an inter-layer adaptation object, not an inter-node adjacency.

answers.gloss: A point at which an external client service accesses the network.
answers.example: The ODU2 customer hand-off at A1.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and provides access for t.cs. It is not independently a tunnel trail head, although an implementation might associate it with an internal tunnel endpoint.

answers.gloss: An externally meaningful end-to-end connectivity service across the network, rather than the internal TE tunnel that might realize it.
answers.example: The requested A1-A3 ODU2 connectivity service.
answers.relations: It uses t.sip access points, is realized through t.cep endpoints, and operates over t.topo.

answers.gloss: A qualifier describing the layer-protocol and multiplexing structure of a signal.
answers.example: ODU2 mapped into an OTU4 server signal.
answers.relations: It qualifies t.cs and is referenced by t.translink adaptation. It does not denote a concrete tributary-slot or TPN allocation.

answers.gloss: A node-local rule group constraining which ports or sides may be internally cross-connected.
answers.example: The permitted ingress-to-egress cross-connect combinations at R2.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and constrains internal switching. Its semantic role is the same kind of permitted-connectivity representation commonly expressed as a connectivity matrix, though this model calls the object a rule group.

answers.gloss: A topological adjacency between two forwarding nodes in the single multi-layer topology; it is not defined as necessarily belonging to a separate layer-specific TE topology.
answers.example: The R1-R2 link.
answers.relations: It is between t.node instances, is terminated by t.ltp instances, and is contained in t.topo.

answers.gloss: One topology instance directly describing the whole multi-layer forwarding domain.
answers.example: The combined OTN-over-optical domain.
answers.relations: It contains t.node and t.link and carries t.cs. Unlike a per-layer topology model, separate topology instances are not required for each layer.

answers.gloss: An endpoint, within a node, of a connection associated with a connectivity service.
answers.example: The endpoint on R1 for the A1-A3 service connection.
answers.relations: It is on t.node, is part of t.cs, and participates in realizing that service. It is not defined specifically as an endpoint belonging to an internal TE tunnel.

proposals.rationale: Both denote a node-owned edge/termination point at which a topological link terminates, and both distinguish that role from service or tunnel endpoints.

Both represent the co-located client/server support or adaptation relationship across layers. The labels differ because A reifies it as an adaptation link while B describes it as a supporting relationship, but the represented relationship is the same.

Both encode node-local constraints or permissions governing which termination points or switching sides may be internally cross-connected. Rule-group versus matrix describes representation or granularity rather than a different switching concept.
